Core Message

Accidents are predictable and preventable — they do not simply happen by chance. Management is ultimately responsible for workplace safety. A systematic approach using planning, organizing, leading, and controlling leads to continuous improvement in safety outcomes.

What is Occupational Health & Safety?

Definition

Occupational Health and Safety (OHS), also called workplace safety, refers to the multidisciplinary field concerned with the safety, health, and welfare of people at work. The goal is to foster a safe and healthy work environment.

Key Principle

Accidents are Predictable Preventable and Not Random. They occur due to identifiable causes — primarily unsafe acts (~80%) or unsafe conditions.

Responsibilities

PartyResponsibility
ManagementEstablish and fund safety programs; set policy; allocate resources; demonstrate commitment
SupervisorsEnforce safety rules; train workers; correct hazards; investigate incidents
EmployeesFollow safety rules; report hazards; use PPE; participate in training

Four Challenges for Practicing Safety

  1. Justifying expenditures — proving ROI of safety programs
  2. Gaining management support — getting top leadership buy-in
  3. Motivating employees — overcoming complacency and resistance
  4. Measuring safety performance — using meaningful metrics beyond injury counts

History of Workplace Safety

Key Historical Milestones

Era / PersonContribution
Code of Hammurabi (~1750 BC)Early legal code with provisions for worker safety in construction; builder held liable for deaths
Hippocrates (400 BC)Linked lead exposure to illness in miners — early occupational medicine
Bernardino Ramazzini (1700)"Father of Occupational Medicine" — wrote De Morbis Artificum Diatriba, cataloguing diseases of tradesmen
Industrial Revolution (1800s)Rise of factory work led to massive injury rates; child labor widespread
Workers' Compensation Laws (early 1900s)Created financial incentives for employers to prevent accidents
OSHA (1970)Occupational Safety and Health Act passed in US; created regulatory framework for workplace safety

Loss Exposures

Speculative Loss Exposure
Offers opportunity for both gain and loss. Example: investing in new machinery — it could break down (loss) or increase productivity (gain).
Pure Loss Exposure
Offers potential for loss only, with no opportunity for gain. Example: a worker getting injured — there is no upside. This is what safety management targets.

Safety Management System (SMS)

Four Safety Management Functions

Planning
Set OHS objectives; identify hazards; assess risks; develop action plans
Organizing
Assign safety responsibilities; allocate resources; establish reporting structures
Leading
Motivate employees; demonstrate management commitment; communicate safety culture
Controlling
Monitor performance; conduct audits; investigate incidents; take corrective actions

ISO 45001 — PDCA for OHS

ISO 45001 is the international standard for Occupational Health and Safety Management Systems. It follows the Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) cycle:

  • Plan: Determine and assess risks; set OHS objectives; plan actions to achieve them
  • Do: Implement the planned actions; manage operational controls; prepare for emergencies
  • Check: Monitor, measure and analyze performance; conduct internal audits
  • Act: Take actions to continually improve; address non-conformities; implement corrective actions

Benefits of an Effective Safety Program

  • Reduces workers' compensation costs and insurance premiums
  • Improves employee morale and retention — workers feel valued
  • Increases productivity — fewer disruptions from accidents/absenteeism
  • Reduces legal liability and regulatory citations
  • Improves company reputation and competitive advantage
  • Protects the company from financial losses due to property damage

Six Core Elements of a Well-Documented Safety Program

  1. Clear management commitment and safety policy
  2. Employee involvement and participation
  3. Worksite analysis (hazard identification)
  4. Hazard prevention and control
  5. Safety and health training
  6. Program evaluation and improvement

Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)

PPE as a Last Resort

PPE sits at the bottom of the hierarchy of controls. The preference is always: Elimination → Substitution → Engineering Controls → Administrative Controls → PPE. PPE is used when other controls are not feasible or as a supplement.

Types of PPE

CategoryExamplesProtects Against
Head ProtectionHard hats, helmetsFalling objects, electrical hazards
Eye/Face ProtectionSafety glasses, goggles, face shieldsChemical splashes, flying particles, radiation
Hearing ProtectionEarplugs, earmuffsNoise above 85 dB TWA
Respiratory ProtectionN95, half/full-face respirators, SCBADust, chemicals, oxygen-deficient atmospheres
Hand/Arm ProtectionGloves (cut-resistant, chemical, heat)Cuts, chemical burns, heat/cold
Foot/Leg ProtectionSteel-toed boots, metatarsal guardsCrush injuries, punctures, chemical spills
Body ProtectionCoveralls, aprons, high-vis vestsChemical exposure, visibility hazards
Fall ProtectionHarnesses, lanyards, lifelinesFalls from heights

Quick Review

What % of accidents are due to unsafe acts vs unsafe conditions?
~80% unsafe acts, ~20% unsafe conditions (Heinrich's finding)
What is the difference between speculative and pure loss exposure?
Speculative: potential for gain AND loss. Pure: potential for loss only (no upside possible).
What are the 4 safety management functions?
Planning, Organizing, Leading, Controlling
What does PDCA stand for in ISO 45001?
Plan, Do, Check, Act — a continuous improvement cycle for OHS
What are the 4 challenges for practicing safety?
Justifying expenditures, gaining management support, motivating employees, measuring performance
Why is PPE the last resort in the hierarchy of controls?
PPE only protects the worker, doesn't eliminate the hazard. Engineering/elimination controls protect everyone automatically without ongoing compliance needed.
Who is called the "Father of Occupational Medicine"?
Bernardino Ramazzini (1700) — wrote the first systematic account of occupational diseases
When was OSHA established and what was its purpose?
Occupational Safety and Health Act, 1970, USA — created federal regulatory framework for workplace safety standards
